title: A single error, located and fixed
sub: Hamming(7,4): 4 data bits, 3 parity bits, and a syndrome that names the flipped position.

frames.caption: Hamming(7,4) sends 4 data bits (1, 0, 1, 1) in 7 positions. The data goes in positions 3, 5, 6 and 7. Positions 1, 2 and 4, the powers of two, are reserved for parity bits.

Each parity bit makes a group of positions have even parity. Bit 1 covers positions {1, 3, 5, 7}; bit 2 covers {2, 3, 6, 7}; bit 4 covers {4, 5, 6, 7}. A position is in a group exactly when that power of two appears in its binary index.
Noise flips one bit in transit: position 6. The receiver does not know which, or whether any bit flipped at all.
Recheck each group. Group 4 ({4, 5, 6, 7}): parity odd, so it failed. Group 2 ({2, 3, 6, 7}): parity odd, so it failed. Group 1 ({1, 3, 5, 7}): parity even.

Read the failed checks as a binary number, the syndrome: 110 in binary is 6. That is exactly the position that flipped, because a flipped bit fails precisely the groups its index belongs to. Flip it back and the data is recovered. Three parity bits can name 7 positions or 'no error': the most a 3-bit syndrome can say, which is why this code is perfect.
